reasoning_content: The goal is to show that the coercion of an indexed infimum of intervals equals the intersection of the coerced intervals. The left-hand side is `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)`. The right-hand side is `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The premise `Interval.coe_iInf` states that for any function `f : ι → Interval α`, the coercion of the infimum of `f` is the intersection of the coerced intervals. Applying this lemma directly to the inner infimum `⨅ j, f i j` would give `↑(⨅ j, f i j) = ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)` for each `i`. However, the goal has an outer infimum over `i`. Using `simp` with `coe_iInf` will rewrite the entire expression stepwise: first, it rewrites `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)` to `⋂ i, ↑(⨅ j, f i j)` by applying the lemma to the outer infimum, and then within each `i`, it rewrites `↑(⨅ j, f i j)` to `⋂ j, ↑(f i j)` by applying the lemma again to the inner infimum. This yields exactly the right-hand side `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The `simp` tactic can handle this nested application because `coe_iInf` is a simp lemma.

The goal is to show that the coercion of a double infimum of intervals equals the double intersection of their coercions. The available lemma `Interval.coe_iInf` simplifies the coercion of a single infimum of intervals to the intersection of their coercions. The expression `⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j` is a nested infimum, which can be rewritten as a single infimum over the product type `Σ i, κ i` using `iInf_and`. Specifically, `iInf_and` states that `⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j = ⨅ p, f p.1 p.2`. Applying this lemma transforms the goal into `↑(⨅ p, f p.1 p.2) = ⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. Now the left-hand side matches the form of `Interval.coe_iInf` with `f` replaced by `fun p => f p.1 p.2`. Applying `coe_iInf` then simplifies the left-hand side to `⋂ p, ↑(f p.1 p.2)`. Finally, `iInf_and` also applies to the right-hand side, rewriting `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)` as `⋂ p, ↑(f p.1 p.2)`, making both sides identical. The `simp` tactic with `coe_iInf` and `iInf_and` performs these rewrites and closes the goal.

The goal is an equality between the coercion of a nested infimum of intervals and a nested intersection of their set coercions. The left-hand side is `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)`. The right-hand side is `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The premise `Interval.coe_iInf` states that for any function `f : ι → Interval α`, the coercion of the infimum equals the intersection of the coercions. Applying this lemma to the inner infimum `⨅ j, f i j` for each fixed `i` would rewrite `↑(⨅ j, f i j)` to `⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. However, the left-hand side is a double infimum, so we first rewrite the entire double infimum as a single infimum over a product type using `iInf_and`. Specifically, `iInf_and` transforms `⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j` into `⨅ p : Σ i, κ i, f p.1 p.2`. Then we can apply `coe_iInf` to this single infimum, which gives `⋂ p, ↑(f p.1 p.2)`. Finally, we rewrite this product intersection back into the nested form `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)` using `iInter_and`. The `simp` tactic with these three lemmas will perform these rewrites in sequence, closing the goal.

The goal is to show that the coercion of an indexed infimum of intervals equals the intersection of the coercions of those intervals. The left-hand side is `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j)`. The right-hand side is `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. The premise `Interval.coe_iInf` states that for any function `f : ι → Interval α`, the coercion of the infimum `⨅ i, f i` equals the intersection `⋂ i, (f i : Set α)`. Here we have a double infimum `⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j`. Applying `coe_iInf` to the outer infimum (with `f` being `λ i => ⨅ j, f i j`) would give `↑(⨅ i, ⨅ j, f i j) = ⋂ i, ↑(⨅ j, f i j)`. Then applying `coe_iInf` again to each inner infimum (with `f` being `λ j => f i j` for each fixed `i`) would give `↑(⨅ j, f i j) = ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`. Substituting this into the previous equality yields the desired result. The `simp` tactic with `[iInf]` in the premise proof simplifies the infimum expressions. Therefore, using `simp only [coe_iInf, iInf]` will apply the lemma to both the outer and inner infima, rewriting the goal to `⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j) = ⋂ i, ⋂ j, ↑(f i j)`, which is trivially true.
